title: "Computational model of aesthetics"
description: "Aesthetic preferences as optimizing a behavioral policy to sample the gradient of a perceptual prior."
toc-depth: 3
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- Aesthetic preferences are modeled as the outcome of optimizing an intrinsic
  (behavioral) policy to sample trajectories for estimating the gradient of a
  perceptual prior, without defining the subjective experience of beauty.
- Building on the [POMDP agent architecture](pomdp-rl.qmd#model-components) and
  the [efficient-encoding motivation for a perceptual
  prior](perceptual-representations.qmd#efficient-encoding-and-the-perceptual-prior),
  the model freezes a useful encoder and separates an extrinsic task policy from
  an intrinsic sampling policy whose trajectories help fit the prior to latents
  encountered under the extrinsic policy.
- The primary candidate model optimizes the intrinsic policy with vanilla
  behavioral policy optimization (BPO) using the gradient of the trajectory-wide
  total negative log-likelihood of the predictive prior; a reverse-KL
  intrinsic-reward alternative is developed on a separate page.
:::

## Overview

Within the [POMDP agent architecture](pomdp-rl.qmd#model-components), this model
starts from a fixed, useful perceptual encoder $F$ and asks how an agent
efficiently learns the normalized perceptual prior $R_\theta(z)$ motivated by
code-complexity control in [Perceptual representations and efficient
encoding](perceptual-representations.qmd#efficient-encoding-and-the-perceptual-prior).
Its central thesis is that aesthetic preferences arise from optimizing a
behavioral (intrinsic) policy to sample trajectories that efficiently estimate
the gradient of that perceptual prior. Rather than defining the subjective
experience of beauty, the model targets the behavioral preferences produced by
this optimization.

Using the shared POMDP components---hidden state $s_t$, observation density $E$,
fixed encoder $F$, memory update $U$, and transition model $T$---the model
splits control into two policies acting on $(z_t, h_t)$:

- **Extrinsic policy $\pi_e$:** optimizes task return and defines the
  distribution of perceptual latents that $R_\theta$ should predict.
- **Intrinsic policy $\pi_i$:** serves as the behavioral sampling policy
  optimized to estimate the gradient of $R_\theta$, hypothesized to give rise to
  aesthetic preferences.

Following the first-version POMDP scope, $F$ and $R_\theta$ take no explicit
temporal-history input while $\pi_e$ and $\pi_i$ condition on $(z_t, h_t)$. This
account is a conceptual hypothesis sitting alongside compression-progress and
predictive-processing theories of aesthetics [@schmidhuber2009; @brielmann2022]:
the mathematical variance-reduction results below justify the sampling
objective without establishing that it accounts for human aesthetics.

## Primary candidate model: vanilla BPO for the prior gradient

In [behavioral policy optimization (BPO)](behavioral-policy-optimization.qmd)
[@papini2024], a behavioral policy is optimized to reduce the variance of
off-policy gradient estimates for a target policy. Here, $\pi_e$ plays the role
of the target policy and $\pi_i$ plays the role of the behavioral policy, while
the vector expectation being estimated shifts from the policy gradient of task
return to the gradient of the perceptual-prior loss on experience generated
under $\pi_e$.

Consider a trajectory of $N$ decision steps from the [POMDP interaction
loop](pomdp-rl.qmd#stimuli-as-consequences-of-actions),

$$
  \tau = (s_0,x_0,z_0,a_0,\dots,a_{N-1},s_N,x_N,z_N),
$$

generated under either policy $\pi \in \{\pi_e,\pi_i\}$ with the same initial
state distribution $\mu_0$, initial memory $h_0$, observation density $E$, fixed
encoder $F$, memory update $U$, and transition model $T$. Write $p_\pi(\tau)$
for the induced trajectory distribution, and hold $\pi_e$, $F$, and the current
prior parameters $\theta$ fixed when optimizing $\pi_i$.

Using the per-step latent surprise $\ell_\theta(z) = -\log R_\theta(z)$, define
the trajectory-wide total negative log-likelihood of the predictive prior as

$$
  \ell_\theta(\tau) = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \ell_\theta(z_t)
                    = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \bigl[-\log R_\theta(z_t)\bigr].
$$

The target prior loss under $\pi_e$ and the single-trajectory gradient estimate
are

$$
  L(\theta) = \mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}\bigl[\ell_\theta(\tau)\bigr],
  \qquad
  g_\theta(\tau) = \nabla_\theta \ell_\theta(\tau)
                 = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \nabla_\theta \bigl[-\log R_\theta(z_t)\bigr].
$$

Assuming differentiation can be exchanged with the expectation,
$\mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}[g_\theta(\tau)] = \nabla_\theta L(\theta)$.

For a trajectory sampled from the intrinsic policy $\tau \sim p_{\pi_i}$, the
importance-weighted prior-gradient estimate is

$$
  \widehat g(\tau) = w(\tau)g_\theta(\tau),
  \qquad
  w(\tau) = \frac{p_{\pi_e}(\tau)}{p_{\pi_i}(\tau)}
          = \prod_{t=0}^{N-1} \frac{\pi_e(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}{\pi_i(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}.
$$

Because $\mu_0$, $E$, $F$, $U$, and $T$ are shared by both policies, they cancel
from the density ratio, leaving only the product of known action probabilities.
Whenever $p_{\pi_i}(\tau) > 0$ on every trajectory with
$p_{\pi_e}(\tau)g_\theta(\tau) \ne 0$ (for instance, when
$\pi_e(\cdot \mid z,h) \ll \pi_i(\cdot \mid z,h)$ along reachable $(z,h)$),
the estimator is unbiased:
$\mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_i}}[\widehat g(\tau)] = \nabla_\theta L(\theta)$.

Theorem 1 of @papini2024 applies to estimating the expectation of any
vector-valued function [@papini2024, fn. 3; see also @alain2016, Theorem 1].
Among unrestricted trajectory distributions $q$, the one minimizing the trace of
the covariance matrix
$\mathbb E_{\tau \sim q}\bigl[\|\widehat g(\tau) - \nabla_\theta L(\theta)\|_2^2\bigr]$
is

$$
  p_\theta^*(\tau) = \frac{p_{\pi_e}(\tau)\|g_\theta(\tau)\|_2}{C_\theta},
  \qquad
  C_\theta = \mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}\bigl[\|g_\theta(\tau)\|_2\bigr],
$$

assuming $0 < C_\theta < \infty$ and finite second moments. Relative to their
probability under $\pi_e$, trajectories whose total prior negative
log-likelihood produces a larger gradient norm are sampled more often.

Because environment dynamics are fixed and $\pi_i$ belongs to a parameterized
policy class $\Pi$, $p_\theta^*$ is generally not realizable. Vanilla BPO
projects $p_\theta^*$ onto realizable trajectory distributions by minimizing the
forward KL divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta^* \Vert p_{\pi_i})$
[@papini2024, sec. 3.2]. Expanding $\log p_{\pi_i}(\tau)$ drops all factors
independent of $\pi_i$ ($\mu_0$, $E$, $F$, $T$), leaving a weighted
cross-entropy objective [@papini2024, Proposition 3.1]:

$$
  \pi_i^* \in \arg\min_{\pi_i \in \Pi}
  \mathbb E_{\tau \sim p_{\pi_e}}\!\left[
    -\|g_\theta(\tau)\|_2 \sum_{t=0}^{N-1} \log \pi_i(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)
  \right].
$$

Because this expectation is taken under $\pi_e$, it can be estimated from
extrinsic trajectories---or off-policy from earlier trajectories via multiple
importance sampling [@papini2024, sec. 3.2]---without estimating unknown latent
marginals or constructing a step-wise intrinsic reward for reinforcement
learning.

Exact variance reduction relative to on-policy sampling depends on
$\chi^2(p_\theta^* \Vert p_{\pi_i})$ rather than forward KL directly
[@papini2024, Lemma 4.1], and without defensive sampling the pure trajectory
weight $w(\tau)$ can grow rapidly with horizon $N$ when $\pi_i$ diverges from
$\pi_e$. Following vanilla BPO [@papini2024, Algorithm 1, Theorem 2],
collecting prior-update trajectories from a defensive mixture
$\Phi = \beta p_{\pi_e} + (1 - \beta)p_{\pi_i}$ with $\beta \in (0,1]$
guarantees support coverage and bounds the importance weight; when
$\|g_\theta(\tau)\|_2$ is also essentially bounded under $p_{\pi_e}$, Theorem 2
of @papini2024 further bounds excess gradient variance in terms of
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta^* \Vert p_{\pi_i})$. For $\tau \sim \Phi$, the
applied importance weight is

$$
  w_\Phi(\tau) = \frac{p_{\pi_e}(\tau)}{\Phi(\tau)}
               = \left[\beta + (1 - \beta)
                 \prod_{t=0}^{N-1} \frac{\pi_i(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}{\pi_e(a_t \mid z_t,h_t)}
                 \right]^{-1}
               \le \frac{1}{\beta}
$$

whenever $p_{\pi_e}(\tau) > 0$ (and $w_\Phi(\tau) = 0$ when
$p_{\pi_e}(\tau) = 0$). Even though $w_\Phi(\tau)$ remains bounded by $1/\beta$
at every horizon, the $N$-step action-probability product inside it can still
concentrate weights near $0$ or $1/\beta$ over long horizons if $\pi_i$ departs
sharply from $\pi_e$, shrinking effective sample size and the variance
reduction gained from $\pi_i$. Moreover, minimizing single-update gradient
variance does not account for correlations across successive prior updates.

## Alternative candidate: reverse-KL intrinsic reward

An alternative formulation operates on single-step latent marginals $p_\pi(z)$
instead of full trajectories, training $\pi_i$ with a reinforcement-learning
intrinsic reward whose expected value under $\pi_i$ minimizes reverse KL
divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\pi_i} \Vert q_\theta^*)$ to the single-sample
variance-optimal latent proposal. Because the ratio of extrinsic to intrinsic
latent marginals is unknown, this route requires a separate density-ratio
estimator and inherits the support-coverage caveats of reverse KL. See
[Reverse-KL intrinsic reward for prior sampling](reverse-kl-prior-sampling.qmd)
for the derivation and feature-based ratio estimator.

## Open questions

- **Horizon scaling and sample allocation:** how do horizon $N$, policy-class
  expressiveness $\Pi$, defensive weight $\beta$, and sample allocation between
  $\pi_e$ and $\pi_i$ affect prior-gradient variance and learning speed, and
  when does importance-weighted sampling outperform on-policy prior learning?
- **Policy scheduling:** when should the agent act under $\pi_e$ versus $\pi_i$,
  and how should $\pi_i$ track simultaneous updates to $\pi_e$ and $\theta$?
- **Empirical signatures:** which behavioral signatures of aesthetic preference
  emerge from optimizing $\pi_i$ for prior-gradient sampling, and how do they
  compare with compression-progress and predictive-processing accounts
  [@schmidhuber2009; @brielmann2022]?
